title: The category-of-simplices last-vertex map is a weak equivalence
statement: Let $K$ be a small simplicial set [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set]. Define $E(K)$ to have objects $([n],x)$ with $x\in K_n$ and arrows $([m],x)\to([n],y)$ the monotone maps $a:[m]\to[n]$ satisfying $K(a)y=x$. Its nerve $NE(K)$ has as $p$-simplices chains of $p$ arrows, with operators given by restriction of chains. For a chain $([n_0],x_0)\xrightarrow{a_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{a_p}([n_p],x_p)$, put $v(i)=a_p\cdots a_{i+1}(n_i)$. The assignment $K(v)x_p\in K_p$ defines a map $\lambda_K:NE(K)\to K$, natural in simplicial maps $K\to L$. This map is a weak homotopy equivalence in the sense of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper].

source.place: Construction 11.9.11.2 and Corollary 11.9.11.5 (retired subsection The Category of Simplices; replaced by Section 6.3.6). No Stacks tag states this homotopy theorem.

proof.text: Composition in $E(K)$ is composition of ordinal maps: if $K(a)y=x$ and $K(b)z=y$, then $K(ba)z=x$. Identities satisfy the same condition. The nerve operators are restriction of functors $[p]\to E(K)$, hence satisfy the simplicial identities. The vertex map $v$ is monotone because $a_{i+1}(n_i)\leq n_{i+1}$. If $\theta:[r]\to[p]$ restricts a chain and $b:[n_{\theta(r)}]\to[n_p]$ is its remaining tail composite, its last-vertex map $v'$ satisfies $bv'=v\theta$, while $x_{\theta(r)}=K(b)x_p$. Thus $K(v')x_{\theta(r)}=K(\theta)K(v)x_p$, proving simpliciality for every operator, including repetitions and omission of the final object. A simplicial map $f:K\to L$ carries $([n],x)$ to $([n],f_nx)$ and leaves the ordinal maps unchanged; $f_pK(v)x_p=L(v)f_{n_p}x_p$. This proves the claimed naturality.

source.place: Construction 11.9.11.2 (01NA) and Corollary 11.9.11.5 (02QS); agent proof by a bisimplicial resolution, rather than the localization theorem used in the published proof.

proof.text: Define a bisimplicial set $W$ by taking $W_{p,q}$ to consist of a chain $c_0\to\cdots\to c_p$ in $E(K)$, where $c_i=([n_i],x_i)$, together with a monotone map $t:[q]\to[n_0]$. Vertical operators precompose $t$. Horizontal operators restrict the chain; when its first object is omitted, replace $t$ by its image under the composite from the old first object to the new first object. This rule satisfies all identities by associativity of ordinal maps and commutes with precomposition of $t$. There are bisimplicial maps $P:W\to A$ and $Q:W\to B$, with $A_{p,q}=NE(K)_p$ constant in $q$, $B_{p,q}=K_q$ constant in $p$: $P$ forgets $t$, and $Q$ takes $K(t)x_0$. Horizontal compatibility of $Q$ is the equation $K(at)y=K(t)K(a)y$; vertical compatibility is functoriality. All sets and indexing categories here are small.

source.place: Construction 11.9.11.2 (01NA) and Corollary 11.9.11.5 (02QS); agent proof by a bisimplicial resolution, rather than the localization theorem used in the published proof.

proof.text: For fixed $p$, $P_{p,\bullet}$ is the coproduct, over its chains, of $\Delta^{n_0}\to\Delta^0$. Identify $\Delta^n$ directly with the nerve of the ordered category $[n]$: in degree $q$ both have the monotone maps $[q]\to[n]$. The unique maps $i\to n$ define a natural transformation from the identity functor of $[n]$ to the constant functor at $n$. By [lem-coef-nerve-natural-homotopy-equivalence], the projection $\Delta^n\to\Delta^0$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. A disjoint union of these maps is again one: the realization quotient relations never change the chain label, and every path, based sphere and based homotopy lies in one summand. Thus $P$ is a vertical weak equivalence in every horizontal degree, also when the chain set is empty.

source.place: Construction 11.9.11.2 (01NA) and Corollary 11.9.11.5 (02QS); agent proof by a bisimplicial resolution, rather than the localization theorem used in the published proof.

proof.text: For fixed $q$, let $C_q$ have objects $([n],x,t)$ with $t:[q]\to[n]$ and arrows $a:([n],x,t)\to([m],y,s)$ satisfying $K(a)y=x$ and $at=s$. Then $W_{\bullet,q}=NC_q$: a chain of these triples is determined by the underlying chain in $E(K)$ and its initial $t$. The value $z=K(t)x$ is constant on arrows, so $C_q$ is the disjoint union of its full categories $C_{q,z}$, $z\in K_q$. Each has initial object $([q],z,\mathrm{id})$, since the unique arrow from it to $([n],x,t)$ is $t$. The unique arrows from this initial object give a natural transformation from its constant functor to the identity. Apply [lem-coef-nerve-natural-homotopy-equivalence] to the projection to the point and the initial-object section. Each $NC_{q,z}\to\Delta^0$ is a weak equivalence. The disjoint-union argument of step 3 proves $Q_{\bullet,q}:W_{\bullet,q}\to\operatorname{const}K_q$ is a weak equivalence, including $K_q=\varnothing$.

source.place: Construction 11.9.11.2 (01NA) and Corollary 11.9.11.5 (02QS); agent proof by a bisimplicial resolution, rather than the localization theorem used in the published proof.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-bisimplicial-diagonal-equivalence] to $P$ using step 3, and to $Q$ using its exchanged-direction assertion and step 4. Since $\operatorname{diag}A=NE(K)$ and $\operatorname{diag}B=K$, obtain weak equivalences $p=\operatorname{diag}P:D\to NE(K)$ and $q=\operatorname{diag}Q:D\to K$, where $D=\operatorname{diag}W$. This invocation does not use either Bousfield--Kan comparison or Thomason's theorem.

source.place: Construction 11.9.11.2 (01NA) and Corollary 11.9.11.5 (02QS); agent proof by a bisimplicial resolution, rather than the localization theorem used in the published proof.

proof.text: Compare $q$ with $\lambda_Kp$ explicitly. On a degree-$r$ element of $D$, put $b=a_r\cdots a_1:[n_0]\to[n_r]$, $u(i)=b(t(i))$, and let $v(i)=a_r\cdots a_{i+1}(n_i)$. Then $q$ takes the value $K(u)x_r$, whereas $\lambda_Kp$ takes $K(v)x_r$. Put $w(i)=\max(u(i),v(i))$. For a simplex $\epsilon:[r]\to[1]$ of $\Delta^1$, define $h_u(i)=u(i)$ if $\epsilon(i)=0$ and $h_u(i)=w(i)$ if $\epsilon(i)=1$. This is monotone: at a switch, $u(i)\leq u(j)\leq w(j)$. The analogous rule with $v$ is monotone too. Both yield maps $D\times\Delta^1\to K$, via $K(h_u)x_r$ and $K(h_v)x_r$, with endpoints $(q,K(w)x_r)$ and $(\lambda_Kp,K(w)x_r)$. To check all operators, restrict by $\theta:[s]\to[r]$ and let $c:[n_{\theta(s)}]\to[n_r]$ be the tail composite. The restricted data give $cu'=u\theta$ and $cv'=v\theta$; since every monotone map preserves binary maximum, $cw'=w\theta$ and $ch'=h\theta$. Together with $x_{\theta(s)}=K(c)x_r$, these equations prove simpliciality, including end-face deletion. By the finite-product preservation of realization in [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits], these simplicial homotopies realize to homotopies with interval $|\Delta^1|=[0,1]$ in k-spaces. They therefore induce homotopies on every compact test cube or sphere: its product with the interval maps continuously to the k-product by its universal property. Thus the realized maps $q$ and $\lambda_Kp$ induce the same component map and conjugate homotopy-group maps under their basepoint paths.

source.place: Construction 11.9.11.2 (01NA) and Corollary 11.9.11.5 (02QS); agent proof by a bisimplicial resolution, rather than the localization theorem used in the published proof.

proof.text: Step 5 says $q$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. The homotopies of step 6 therefore imply that $\lambda_Kp$ is one as well: its component map agrees with that of $q$, and the change-of-basepoint isomorphism along the homotopy path identifies their homotopy-group maps. Finally the model structure in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] gives two-out-of-three for weak homotopy equivalences; since $p$ and $\lambda_Kp$ are weak equivalences, so is $\lambda_K$. For $K=\varnothing$, all resolution sets and both source and target of $\lambda_K$ are empty, so the same argument includes this case.
